title: Roman imperial rule: Augustus to Diocletian

interval.label: 27 BCE–284 CE · an early imperial frame
interval.note: This orientation ends with Diocletian’s accession, not the end of Rome. The featured Severan case remains 193–235 CE.

summary: The Severans came after two centuries of imperial government. Changes of ruling family did not create a new society each time; the court, army, provinces and cities continued to interact.

phases.title: Augustus
phases.text: The Senate grants Octavian the title Augustus. Republican offices continue within a political system dominated by an emperor.

phases.title: A new ruling family
phases.text: Septimius Severus wins power through civil conflict. This is the start of the focused case, not of the empire.

phases.title: Citizenship expands
phases.text: Caracalla extends citizenship broadly among the empire’s free inhabitants. Legal inclusion does not mean equal power.

phases.title: The Severan dynasty ends
phases.text: Alexander Severus is killed; Roman imperial government continues through repeated struggles over succession.

phases.title: A different arrangement of power
phases.text: Diocletian becomes emperor and later reorganizes administration and imperial leadership.

citations.locator: Diocletian, Constantine, and the Late Empire

title: Han, interruption and restoration

interval.label: 206 BCE–220 CE · Han with the Xin interruption
interval.note: A conventional broad frame. Han rule was interrupted; the featured Eastern Han period is 25–220 CE.

summary: An imperial tradition can survive a change of capital and a break in dynastic rule. Earlier arguments about farming and government help explain institutions, but must be dated separately from the later tomb models.

citations.locator: Western Han and Eastern Han paragraphs

phases.title: Western Han begins
phases.text: The museum’s conventional chronology begins in 206 BCE. Chang’an becomes the western capital.

phases.title: Grain and government
phases.text: Chao Cuo proposes using rewards and rank to encourage grain deliveries to the state.

phases.title: A disagreement at court
phases.text: Officials and scholars debate state monopolies and the resources needed for frontier defense.

phases.title: The interruption
phases.text: Wang Mang’s Xin regime interrupts Han rule. The broad frame is not one uninterrupted dynasty.

citations.locator: Transition between Western and Eastern Han

phases.title: Eastern Han
phases.text: Restored Han rulers govern from Luoyang. The architectural models belong to this later setting.

phases.title: Dynastic rule ends
phases.text: The Han period ends; this boundary does not end Chinese communities, farming or cultural traditions.

title: A landscape made and remade

interval.label: Approximately ninth–fifteenth centuries CE
interval.note: Capital-era orientation only. Angkor Wat’s religious use and local habitation continue beyond this frame.

summary: Reservoirs, temples and settlements accumulated across many reigns. The phase labels below are broad periods, not exact construction dates for every feature.

citations.locator: The Life History of the Angkor Wat Temple

phases.label: Ninth century
phases.title: Successive centers
phases.text: Early centers and water works precede the most familiar stone monuments.

phases.label: Eleventh century
phases.title: West Baray
phases.text: A major reservoir adds to a landscape already shaped by earlier projects.

phases.label: Early twelfth century
phases.title: Angkor Wat
phases.text: The temple associated with Suryavarman II forms part of a wider inhabited landscape.

citations.locator: The Life History of the Angkor Wat Temple

phases.label: Late twelfth century
phases.title: Reorganization
phases.text: New projects, including the Jayatataka reservoir, modify the network rather than starting it anew.

phases.label: Fourteenth–fifteenth centuries
phases.title: Stress and transformation
phases.text: Climate variability, infrastructure damage and changing political and economic relationships form overlapping explanations.

title: Partition before and after August 1947

interval.label: 1945–1950 · a selected transition and aftermath
interval.note: A teaching window, not the lifespan of India or Pakistan and not an end date for displacement or memory.

summary: Negotiations, violence, independence, boundary announcements and rebuilding home occurred on different timetables. The 1947 case stays dated 1947; this wider frame makes the aftermath visible at 1950.

phases.title: An official explanation
phases.text: A British official’s notes explain conflict through “communal” differences and defend British rule. That framing is itself evidence to examine.

phases.title: An appeal before the border
phases.text: Santokh Singh writes about Sikh concerns in June 1946, before the eventual boundary is known.

phases.label: 3 June 1947
phases.title: The partition plan
phases.text: Mountbatten, Nehru and Jinnah announce a transfer to two governments on an accelerated timetable.

phases.label: 14–17 August 1947
phases.title: Independence, then the boundary announcement
phases.text: Independence ceremonies on 14/15 August precede the announcement of the boundary awards on 17 August.

phases.label: September 1947
phases.title: Movement and violence continue
phases.text: The High Commissioner reports attacks on refugee groups travelling in both directions in Punjab.

phases.title: A later departure in Bengal
phases.text: The museum’s account of Ila Banerjee describes her family leaving in 1950. This is one testimony, not a date for all migration from Bengal.

title: Indonesia: revolution, recognition and the form of the state

interval.label: Selected transition, 1945–1950
interval.note: A bounded reference frame, not the lifetime of Indonesia or an end to all disputes.

summary: Independence was proclaimed in 1945, contested through war and diplomacy, recognized in a federal transfer in 1949 and followed by a unitary state in 1950.

phases.label: 17 August 1945
phases.title: Proclamation
phases.text: Sukarno and Hatta proclaim independence in Jakarta.

phases.label: July 1947
phases.title: Dutch offensive
phases.text: The first major Dutch offensive is officially described as a “police action”; the term obscures the colonial war.

phases.label: December 1948
phases.title: Yogyakarta taken
phases.text: A second offensive takes the Republican capital and arrests leaders; the conflict continues.

phases.label: 27 December 1949
phases.title: Federal transfer
phases.text: The Netherlands transfers sovereignty to a federal United States of Indonesia, excluding Netherlands New Guinea.

phases.title: Unitary republic
phases.text: The federal arrangement is replaced by a unitary state. The New Guinea dispute remains outside this settlement.

title: Ghana: organizing, independence and the early republic

interval.label: Selected political sequence, 1948–1964
interval.note: The reference frame extends beyond the 1948–1960 case to show the later one-party turn; it is not Ghana’s full history.

summary: Mobilization and elections increased African control of government before independence in 1957. A republic followed in 1960; opposition rights require their own history.

phases.title: Unrest and constitutional inquiry
phases.text: Postwar grievances and unrest prompt a new constitutional process.

phases.title: CPP formed
phases.text: Nkrumah establishes a new party seeking immediate self-government.

phases.title: Election and entry into government
phases.text: The CPP wins; Nkrumah leaves prison to lead government business under a colonial constitutional framework.

phases.label: 6 March 1957
phases.title: Independence
phases.text: Ghana becomes independent, initially retaining the monarchy.

phases.label: 1 July 1960
phases.title: Republic
phases.text: A president replaces the monarch as head of state.

phases.title: One-party state
phases.text: Constitutional change formalizes one-party rule. This later milestone qualifies a story that stops with liberation.

title: South Africa: apartheid rule and a constitutional transition

interval.label: Selected frame, 1948–1997
interval.note: Apartheid intensified earlier segregation. This frame ends at constitutional commencement, not the end of inequality or South African history.

summary: Resistance and negotiations led to the 1994 election and a constitution that bound government to rights. Adoption, Court review, signing and commencement were separate steps.

phases.title: Apartheid government
phases.text: The National Party comes to power and intensifies racial segregation and exclusion.

phases.title: Interim settlement
phases.text: An interim constitutional arrangement provides a framework for the election and for drafting a new constitution.

phases.label: April 1994
phases.title: Democratic election
phases.text: The election brings a Government of National Unity and elected representatives who also undertake constitution-making.

phases.label: 8 May 1996
phases.title: Text adopted
phases.text: Assembly adoption is followed by a required Constitutional Court certification process.

phases.label: October 1996
phases.title: Text amended
phases.text: Amendments follow Court review.

phases.label: 10 December 1996
phases.title: Signed at Sharpeville
phases.text: Mandela signs the constitution.

phases.label: 4 February 1997
phases.title: Comes into effect
phases.text: Commencement is a distinct milestone from signing.

title: Uruk: urban growth and later city-states

interval.label: c. 3300–2350 BCE: selected urban and Early Dynastic orientation
interval.note: A bounded teaching frame spanning later-fourth-millennium growth and the conventional 2900–2350 BCE Early Dynastic period; neither boundary is the lifespan of Uruk.

summary: Place the tablet within a city that grew before it and continued afterward. Urban institutions, later walls and changing rulers have separate chronologies.

citations.locator: Urban growth and Early Dynastic paragraphs
Ergebnisse: late Uruk buildings and walls

phases.label: Later fourth millennium BCE
phases.title: Urban growth before the selected object
phases.text: The frame opens within the era of expanding settlements and monumental building. It is not a foundation year.

phases.label: Around 3200 BCE
phases.title: A large urban centre
phases.text: The museum describes monumental mud-brick construction, crafts and institutional accounting at Uruk.

phases.label: c. 3100–2900 BCE
phases.title: The selected grain account
phases.text: This is the object’s date range. Its provenance is only probably Uruk; the account reading remains qualified.

phases.label: c. 2900–2350 BCE
phases.title: Early Dynastic city-states
phases.text: Later political changes, walls and traditions about rulers belong to the continuing city, not to a securely identified author of the selected tablet.

title: Dholavira: a changing settlement within the Indus world

interval.label: c. 3000–1500 BCE occupation orientation
interval.note: UNESCO’s broad site range is retained. The GPR paper gives an approximate 1700 BCE endpoint; phase anchors below are broad orientation labels, not independently dated construction events.

summary: The city changed in layout and use over a long occupation. The regional seal has a narrower date range; the plan is a modern composite, not one frozen urban moment.

phases.label: From around 3000 BCE
phases.title: Early occupation
phases.text: UNESCO traces the earliest settlement evidence to this approximate date. Later urban features are not all assigned to it.

phases.label: c. 2600–1900 BCE: regional object range
phases.title: The seal’s narrower window
phases.text: The selected Met seal is dated within the broader occupation. Its Indus Valley attribution does not make it a find from Dholavira.

phases.label: Across the third and second millennia BCE
phases.title: Changing spaces and activities
phases.text: Excavation records growth, change and later contraction. The orientation anchor does not date every reservoir, house or workshop to 2000 BCE.

phases.label: c. 1500 BCE: UNESCO range endpoint
phases.title: An approximate end to this site frame
phases.text: The shorter c. 1700 BCE endpoint in the radar paper remains visible as a source difference. Neither is treated as one precisely dated collapse event.

title: Liangzhu: city, dams and objects on different clocks

interval.label: c. 3300–2300 BCE site orientation
interval.note: The site frame follows UNESCO. Dam distributions in calibrated BP are not exact phase boundaries; the Met’s c3200–2000 BCE culture label has a wider endpoint.

summary: Waterworks developed in phases within a rice-producing landscape. A city frame, dam samples and an individual jade must remain separate chronological units.

phases.label: c. 3300 BCE: site frame opens
phases.title: A regional landscape
phases.text: The World Heritage frame encompasses the city, waterworks and differentiated cemeteries. It does not date every feature to the opening year.

phases.label: c. 3250–2850 BCE: approximate conversion
phases.title: High-dam sample cluster
phases.text: The paper reports most high-dam results at 5200–4800 calibrated BP. Subtracting from the 1950 BP baseline gives this rounded BCE orientation; outliers and construction phases remain.

phases.label: c. 3050–2850 BCE: approximate conversion
phases.title: Low dams and levees
phases.text: Most low-dam/levee dates cluster at 5000–4800 calibrated BP. Overlapping date distributions do not prove simultaneous construction.

phases.label: Around 2400 BCE
phases.title: The selected cong
phases.text: The museum dates this object separately and does not identify it as a city excavation find.

phases.label: Around 2300 BCE
phases.title: The site orientation ends
phases.text: This is the UNESCO range endpoint, not the disappearance of every community or all Liangzhu cultural forms.

title: Hattusha: settlement, capital and transformation

interval.label: c. 2000–1180 BCE: selected settlement and capital orientation
interval.note: The frame opens before the Hittite capital and ends with an approximate capital-era endpoint in the DAI overview. It is not the settlement’s entire lifespan or one exact destruction date.

summary: The original 13th-century inquiry remains a case within a longer institutional and settlement history. Gordion’s drought record and the capital’s political transition have their own dates and limits.

phases.label: Before the Hittite capital (orientation)
phases.title: Earlier settlement and trade
phases.text: The excavated residential sequence extends from the kārum period into Hittite phases. The viewing year is an approximate orientation, not a source date for a specific house or the late royal administration.

phases.label: From around 1650 BCE
phases.title: A capital and cult centre
phases.text: The DAI’s broad capital orientation begins here, with palace, temples and archives as institutional evidence. It does not imply an unchanging court or uniform occupation.

phases.label: 13th century BCE, approaching c. 1200
phases.title: The preserved case window
phases.text: The dossier’s original interval remains unchanged. The overall city plan must still be read as a composite of phases.

phases.label: Around 1198–1196 BCE (±3 years)
phases.title: A severe dry episode in the Gordion record
phases.text: The central estimate follows the approximate case endpoint. Its three-year uncertainty can overlap that boundary. It supplies a possible environmental stress, not an exact year for every institutional ending.

phases.label: Around 1180 BCE: broad orientation endpoint
phases.title: Capital-era transition, with later lives
phases.text: The project overview’s capital frame ends approximately here. Royal withdrawal, later burning and continued settlement histories must not be merged into the disappearance of a whole population.

title: Uluburun within eastern Mediterranean exchange

interval.label: c. 1500–1200 BCE: selected exchange orientation
interval.note: An authored regional teaching window around the wreck and later transformations, not the lifespan of one trade network or a confirmed shipping itinerary.

summary: Place a single shipment within a wider history of manufacture, transport and exchange. Objects travelled together, but proposed origins and routes require separate arguments.

phases.label: Later second millennium BCE
phases.title: Production and exchange before the wreck
phases.text: The frame opens within a period of regional movement of raw materials and finished goods. No single founding event for a unified network is asserted.

phases.label: c. 1335–1305 BCE: the case envelope
phases.title: An approximate wreck window
phases.text: These bounds express the INA account’s c1320 BCE ±15 estimate. They do not identify the exact year of sailing or sinking.

phases.label: Around 1320 BCE (±15 years)
phases.title: One cargo association
phases.text: Copper, tin, containers and other goods were recovered in association with a hull and anchors. Not every recovery position is an original stowage position.

phases.label: Around 1200 BCE
phases.title: A later set of regional transformations
phases.text: The earlier wreck cannot prove all maritime exchange stopped at this later date or explain every political transition.

title: Shang institutions and the late capital at Yin Xu

interval.label: c. 1600–1046 BCE: conventional Shang orientation
interval.note: The wider period convention is distinct from Yin Xu’s c1300–1046 BCE frame and the dates/provenance of individual objects. Neither selected Met object is assigned to an excavated royal tomb.

summary: Separate a dynasty label, a late capital, divination practices and specific objects. Their overlapping dates do not make them one archive or one documented workshop.

phases.label: Around 1600 BCE: conventional period start
phases.title: The broader Shang frame
phases.text: This is the museum period convention, not the founding date of the late capital or a narrow date for the selected bone.

phases.label: c. 1300–1046 BCE
phases.title: The late-capital orientation
phases.text: Yin Xu’s palace/ancestral shrine and royal tomb areas provide dated archaeological contexts within the broader period.

phases.label: Within the 13th–11th centuries BCE
phases.title: The selected pouring vessel
phases.text: The gong’s date is broad and its Anyang attribution qualified. This viewing anchor does not date a known casting event to 1200 BCE.

phases.label: Around 1046 BCE: conventional transition
phases.title: A different political transition
phases.text: The Met chronology places the Shang–Zhou change here, later than the transformations around 1200 in Anatolia. It is not evidence for one global collapse.

title: Qin projects, imperial rule and local records

interval.label: c. 246–206 BCE: selected Qin project and imperial orientation
interval.note: Opens with the mausoleum project’s reported start, not the founding of Qin. Case and alternate dynasty conventions remain separate.

summary: A royal project began before imperial unification; the Liye archive has its own narrower dates. Do not turn one period label into the date of every object or document.

phases.label: From around 246 BCE
phases.title: A royal project before the imperial frame
phases.text: UNESCO dates the beginning of the mausoleum project here. The tomb and capital are different places.

phases.label: 222–208 BCE: document range
phases.title: The local records have their own clock
phases.text: Staack dates most of the Liye documents to this range, beginning before the dossier’s imperial frame.

phases.label: 221 BCE: imperial unification convention
phases.title: A common standard is announced
phases.text: The capacity measure’s decree is attributed to the First Emperor’s 26th year. It is not the production date of all measuring devices.

phases.label: 210 BCE
phases.title: The First Emperor’s death
phases.text: The death of a ruler, the end of his dynasty and the end of local administrative work are different boundaries.

phases.label: 207/206 BCE: different dynasty conventions
phases.title: Preserve the difference
phases.text: The Met’s 206 endpoint remains in the case; the National Palace Museum and Staack use 207. The atlas does not silently resolve that convention.

title: Mauryan rule and Ashoka’s regional messages

interval.label: c. 320–185 BCE: selected Mauryan orientation
interval.note: Rounded opening within the late-fourth-century setting described by Neelis; not a new exact accession date. Later succession traditions differ.

summary: Place Ashoka’s reign within a longer dynasty and distinguish a regnal reference, a particular inscription and later traditions.

phases.label: Late fourth century BCE (orientation)
phases.title: A dynasty before Ashoka
phases.text: Neelis describes Chandragupta taking power from the Nandas at Pataliputra. The viewing year is a rounded orientation, not an exact date supplied by that account.

phases.label: c. 268–232 BCE
phases.title: The preserved reign convention
phases.text: The original dossier keeps Neelis’s dates. Inscriptions use relative regnal dates and do not all belong to one calendar year.

phases.label: Eighth regnal year; approximately 260 BCE
phases.title: Kalinga in a royal account
phases.text: This approximate viewing year derives from the retained reign convention. Edict XIII expresses remorse; Dhauli’s local set has different passages.

phases.label: Mid-third century BCE (viewing anchor)
phases.title: Read particular messages
phases.text: Girnar II, Dhauli Separate I and Kandahar language evidence have separate settings. This anchor does not assign them all an exact issue date of 250 BCE.

phases.label: Around 185 BCE
phases.title: A later political transition
phases.text: Neelis describes the overthrow of the last Mauryan ruler while noting differing succession traditions. It is not the endpoint of the life of Ashoka’s inscriptions.

title: Athens: changing civic rules and public work

interval.label: Sixth–fourth centuries BCE: selected civic/work orientation
interval.note: Matches the analytical case window while separating the vase, changing eligibility rules and later procedural account. Neither boundary is the lifespan of Athens or democracy.

summary: The Archaic vase, fifth-century rules and fourth-century institutional description are different evidence within a broad teaching window.

phases.label: c. 510–500 BCE
phases.title: The selected water jar
phases.text: The Met vessel’s approximate date straddles a political transition; its scene is not an image of the later constitution.

phases.label: Around 508 BCE: conventional marker
phases.title: An institutional transition
phases.text: The Agora authors use this conventional democracy marker to distinguish their earlier vase from later texts. Institutions continued to change.

phases.label: 451/0 BCE
phases.title: A rule about civic descent
phases.text: Forsdyke dates the two-parent citizenship rule here. Female civic descent and male formal participation must not be collapsed into one role.

phases.label: 403 BCE
phases.title: A rule reestablished
phases.text: Forsdyke describes the parentage law’s reestablishment after interruption. The same eligibility rule was not simply unchanged across the whole case.

phases.label: Around 330 BCE
phases.title: The later procedural account
phases.text: The Constitution of the Athenians describes institutions of its own period while also narrating earlier changes. This is not the date of the selected jar.

title: Palmyra: families, civic rules and changing power

interval.label: First–third centuries CE: selected civic orientation
interval.note: Rounded teaching frame, not Palmyra’s foundation or disappearance. The memorial retains its separate second–third-century date range.

summary: Distinguish family memorials, civic transactions and caravan commemoration within a city that continued after third-century conflict.

phases.label: Mid-first century CE (orientation)
phases.title: A trading city in a wider setting
phases.text: The Met describes Palmyra’s prosperity and caravan setting by this period. This viewing point is not an exact foundation date.

phases.label: 137 CE
phases.title: A public fiscal decision
phases.text: A council decree and revised tariff address recurring charges. The regulation’s civic scope is distinct from caravan itineraries.

phases.label: Second–third centuries CE: object window
phases.title: The selected family memorial
phases.text: The broad catalogue range does not identify an exact year for carving, commissioning or the deaths represented.

phases.label: 272 CE
phases.title: Aurelian recaptures Palmyra
phases.text: The Getty account distinguishes this siege from the following year’s conflict. The portrait is not evidence of the family’s role in either event.

phases.label: 273 CE
phases.title: Another siege and later habitation
phases.text: A second rebellion and siege damaged the city. The same account describes continued habitation afterward; this is not a date of complete disappearance.

title: Kushan rule: coin images, temple orders and maintenance

interval.label: First–third centuries CE: selected Kushan frame
interval.note: Analytical orientation, not newly asserted foundation/dissolution dates. Absolute ruler chronology and some inscription readings remain debated.

summary: Keep an era’s proposed starting point, events described retrospectively, object catalogues and later building works on separate clocks.

phases.label: Possibly c. 104/105 CE
phases.title: A date in an unnamed era
phases.text: Sims-Williams discusses a possible conversion of Dasht-e Nawur’s year 279 and identifies Vima Taktu. The conversion depends on the proposed era and remains conditional.

phases.label: c. 127/128 CE: proposed era start
phases.title: A chronology used for comparison
phases.text: The editor and Berlin catalogue use this revised framework. It does not turn every accession or coin date into an exact settled year.

phases.label: Probably no earlier than c. 132/133 CE
phases.title: The Rabatak record
phases.text: The text remembers first-year events but may refer to year six. A lower bound on the record differs from the date of its narrated commands.

phases.label: Not before c. 158/159 CE
phases.title: Surkh Kotal and water works
phases.text: The editor dates the works’ year 31 in this proposed absolute framework. The inscription itself may be later, and technical readings remain qualified.

title: Aksum, Adulis and inland work through time

interval.label: First–seventh centuries CE: selected connections and excavated phases
interval.note: A reference window for these sources, not exact founding/abandonment or the full lifespan of Aksum. The original dossier retains its first–eighth-century convention.

summary: An early port account, fourth-century royal writing and later inland deposits describe different phases. They do not all illustrate 200 CE.

phases.label: Mid-first century CE (viewing anchor)
phases.title: The merchant-oriented account
phases.text: The Periplus discussion places Adulis and inland exchange in this period; the viewing year is not a precise composition date or an imperial border.

phases.label: 200 CE: chapter viewing anchor
phases.title: Keep later evidence dated
phases.text: The chapter opens a changing world. The major stelae and the reproduced excavated coins retain later dates; none is silently assigned to this exact year.

phases.label: Fourth century CE (orientation)
phases.title: Royal writing and changing religion
phases.text: Greek and Ge’ez occur in multiple scripts. The excavation study places Ezana’s conversion broadly in the mid-fourth century while cautioning about its non-elite effects.

phases.label: Late sixth–seventh-century deposits
phases.title: Coins and everyday work
phases.text: The excavation combines coin types, pottery and radiocarbon evidence to interpret later deposits. Armah’s proposed dates have an alternative discussed in the source.

phases.label: Around the mid-seventh century CE
phases.title: Latest dated occupation in this excavation
phases.text: The latest dated charcoal samples inform a phase of habitation. This rounded viewing point does not establish the last resident’s departure or the end of the kingdom.

title: Chang’an before, within and after the Tang frame

interval.label: Sui rebuilding and Tang capital: selected phases, 581–907 CE
interval.note: A reference window for these sources, not the lifespan of Xi’an or a claim that all fabric dates to 581.

summary: A rebuilt Sui capital, Tang government, religious translation and later disruptions have separate dates.

phases.label: 581 onward: Sui accession and rebuilding
phases.title: A new capital follows an older city
phases.text: The source places the decision to build a new capital under the Sui; this viewing year marks that transition, not a fully completed city.

phases.label: 618 CE
phases.title: Tang dynastic frame begins
phases.text: An inherited urban and institutional setting precedes the new dynasty.

phases.label: 645 CE
phases.title: Xuanzang returns with texts
phases.text: The return differs from the following work of translation and storage.

phases.label: 652 CE; rebuilding 701–704
phases.title: A pagoda has more than one date
phases.text: A first foundation does not date all the standing structure.

phases.label: Mid-eighth century: orientation
phases.title: Rebellion and weakened authority
phases.text: This viewing anchor locates a major disruption; the dynasty continued afterward.

phases.label: 845 CE
phases.title: Religious persecutions
phases.text: The account describes persecution affecting multiple religious communities. Prior presence did not guarantee lasting security.

phases.label: 907 CE: conventional dynastic endpoint
phases.title: A dynasty ends; a city continues changing
phases.text: This is not Xi’an’s final date or the date of every later monument.

title: Abbasid-era Iraq: capitals, workshops and changing control

interval.label: 750–1258 CE: selected Iraq-centered phases
interval.note: A teaching frame matching the conventional dynastic case, not uninterrupted uniform sovereignty or the full history of Iraqi cities.

summary: Baghdad and Samarra, production evidence and a dated manuscript belong to different moments within changing political authority.

phases.label: 750 CE
phases.title: Abbasid rule begins
phases.text: This precedes Baghdad’s foundation.

phases.label: 762 CE
phases.title: Baghdad is founded
phases.text: The new capital concentrates political and cultural activity.

phases.label: 836–892 CE
phases.title: The court at Samarra
phases.text: A capital phase differs from the whole dynastic span and from the selected tenth-century bowl.

phases.label: 945 CE
phases.title: Buyid control of Baghdad
phases.text: Caliphal authority changes; later Seljuq control begins in 1055.

phases.label: 621 AH / 1224 CE
phases.title: A manuscript is copied and illustrated
phases.text: The dated leaf is attributed to Baghdad; this is not a first translation date or observed hospital scene.

phases.label: 1258 CE
phases.title: Mongol sack of Baghdad
phases.text: This endpoint does not retrospectively make earlier political control uniform; later nominal caliphs in Egypt fall outside this case.

title: Nalanda: institutional history, an account and conserved remains

interval.label: Fifth–thirteenth centuries CE: monastic and scholastic frame
interval.note: Rounded century boundaries; earlier archaeological remains and modern conservation retain separate dates. No exact foundation or destruction year is asserted.

summary: The institutional frame, seventh-century textual evidence and a modern photograph answer different questions.

phases.label: Fifth century CE: rounded boundary
phases.title: A monastic and scholastic institution
phases.text: UNESCO distinguishes the institutional frame from earlier archaeology at the site.

phases.label: Later seventh century CE: viewing anchor
phases.title: Yijing describes practices
phases.text: This approximate viewing year places selected accounts; it is not a precise observation date for every passage or building.

phases.label: Thirteenth century CE: rounded orientation
phases.title: Sack and abandonment in the broad synthesis
phases.text: The source uses a century-scale account. This viewing point is not an exact destruction date.

phases.label: End of the selected century-scale frame
phases.title: Keep later excavation separate
phases.text: Excavation, conservation and the 2023 photograph are modern episodes, not the medieval institution’s continuation.

title: Song institutions: northern and southern phases

interval.label: 960–1279 CE: Northern and Southern Song
interval.note: Conventional dynastic frame; distinct neighboring states and changing control remain. It is not the lifespan of all Chinese institutions.

summary: The two capital phases, a 1069 proposal and an independently dated bowl remain distinct.

phases.label: 960 CE: conventional beginning
phases.title: Northern Song frame
phases.text: The capital setting is Kaifeng; neighboring Liao and later Jin histories remain distinct.

phases.label: 1069 CE
phases.title: Crop loans are proposed

title: Western Mexico: architecture, offerings and regional communities

interval.note: Uses López Mestas’s 2026 Late Preclassic/Early Classic orientation, not the lifespan or borders of one Colima state. summary: People made architectural miniatures and prepared funerary places within varied western Mexican communities. A possible vessel lid, regional offering traditions and a documented excavation reveal different parts of that work.

phases.label: Around 300 BCE: beginning of the selected regional frame
phases.title: Shared mortuary forms did not require one state
phases.text: López Mestas describes western Mexican communities through a 300 BCE–400 CE orientation. This is a regional interpretation of social relationships, not a founding date, common constitution or political border for everyone called Colima.

phases.text: The current Met record attributes this ceramic model to Colima and gives a broad 200 BCE–200 CE range. phases.label: First century CE: the separately excavated Huitzilapa tomb
phases.title: An excavation supplies an association
phases.text: The 1996 excavators report radiocarbon clustering in the first century CE at Huitzilapa, in central Jalisco. These are site-specific findings; the original laboratory tables were not consulted, and no object route or Huitzilapa origin is assigned to the Colima model.

phases.title: A teaching frame is not a universal ending
phases.text: The selected reference follows the 2026 essay’s regional endpoint. The INAH Colima account has its own wider shaft-tomb orientation and a local Comala convention of 200–400 CE. title: Ohio gathering and earthwork construction

phases.title: A wider orientation keeps its source
phases.text: York’s 2023 article describes a Hopewell religious movement approximately 100 BCE–500 CE. These are attributed frames with different scopes, not a founding date or one people’s complete lifespan.

phases.title: Buildings, gatherings and later mound additions
phases.text: NPS places Mound City construction within this broad interval. Its account describes a ceremonial building and clay floor, deliberate dismantling and earthen additions. phases.title: A sampled wall has a narrower dating question
phases.text: The NPS account of 2001–02 investigations associates burned logs in one trench with initial construction of one Hopeton enclosure wall around 300 CE. phases.title: A teaching bound does not end Indigenous presence

title: Constantinople: portable images and harbour work

interval.label: 843–1204 CE: a selected Middle Byzantine reference frame
interval.note: Follows Brooks’s Middle Byzantine convention, with the substantive urban inquiry bounded to ninth–eleventh-century evidence. This is not a new lifespan or territorial boundary for Byzantium: the complete original case remains 330–1453, including Latin rule in Constantinople during 1204–1261. Earlier timber evidence may predate this reference frame; a phase marker is not a precise construction, sinking or production year.

summary: An ivory panel and separately excavated ship timbers reveal carving, fitting, joining and repair in a working capital. Object interpretation, archaeological context and political change answer different questions.

citations.locator: Ivory images in the tenth–eleventh centuries

phases.label: 843: images return after the second iconoclastic episode
phases.title: A period convention follows a contested practice
phases.text: Brooks distinguishes image controversies in 726–787 and 815–843 and describes the reintroduction of images in 843. Icons appeared in different materials and settings, while their relationship to sacred subjects was debated. This boundary organizes a reference period; it does not mean every image, viewer or workshop followed one uninterrupted practice.

phases.title: One wreck has several chronological questions
phases.text: The excavators initially associated YK14 with pottery dated to the late ninth or early tenth century. Wood dating and a timber likely associated with the ship suggested construction in the first half of the ninth century, potentially before this reference begins. Fitted planks and repeated repairs belong to its material history. The marker 900 is an approximate orientation to the reported context, not an exact construction, repair or sinking year. No cargo or ballast was recovered.

title: Central Java: religious buildings, stories and support

phases.title: Religious narratives represented in local settings
phases.text: Santiko’s abstract interprets Karmawibhangga through religious-text comparison and Javanese cultural adaptation, using a ninth–tenth-century frame. This is a study-specific interpretive setting, not a new construction date or an independently verified date for every depicted building.

phases.text: BorobudurPedia connects Tri Tepusan, Sri Kahulunan and land privileges for a religious foundation with Borobudur. interval.label: Selected Classic-period orientation, c. 250–900 CE

summary: Potters, artists, patrons and households connected made objects with food, representation and exchange. A named owner’s cup and separately documented household and painter contexts reveal different scales of that work.

title: Chaco communities: building, provisioning and circulation

phases.title: Smaller habitation and storage spaces enter the frame
phases.text: The NPS Pueblo-period account describes smaller habitation compounds alongside later great houses, with storage rooms, pithouses, outdoor shelters and additions. phases.text: NPS places Pueblo Bonito’s planned construction in stages across roughly three centuries. Rubble cores, faced masonry and varied spaces involved different materials and tasks. phases.text: The retained 2009 study consultation records five vessel-fragment samples, three positive probable cylinder jars and stylistic dates around 1000–1125. phases.text: NPS describes slower new construction and changing regional roles in these centuries, with migration and connections to other places. interval.label: Selected neighborhood and making evidence, c. 1050–1200 CE

summary: Homes, public buildings and craft debris help reveal urban relationships. Unfinished copper and a local soil test connect particular materials with particular questions, without making one photo or proxy a complete history of the city and its people.

phases.title: Settlement includes more than a monumental core
phases.text: The retained Illinois source scope places organized earthmoving and urban reorganization around 1050. These are specific places within Greater Cahokia, not a border around every Mississippian community or proof of one household form.

citations.locator: Retained 27 October scope: urban core and reorganization

phases.label: Late eleventh century: neighborhoods being created and reconfigured
phases.title: A building pattern needs an interpretation
phases.text: Betzenhauser and Pauketat compare architectural diversity, density, placement and craft-production debris in neighborhoods at Cahokia and East St. Louis. The marker 1100 orients the reported late-eleventh-century frame; it is not an exact construction year, count of residents or recovered household roster.

phases.title: Small unfinished pieces reveal a working process
phases.text: The 2011 copper paper attributes a workshop-house context to the early Moorehead phase around 1200 through previous field reports. Metallographic observations and modern comparisons support an interpretation of repeated hammering and annealing; they do not date each piece precisely or identify a named worker. title: Ocmulgee: public buildings and a changing settlement history

interval.note: A source-qualified research frame for selected buildings and settlement evidence, not an Earthlodge construction/use interval. summary: Built gathering places, household work and retained archaeological collections support different inquiries. phases.text: The authors discuss Council Chamber 2 as approximately contemporary with the Earthlodge, while its model remains imprecise. phases.title: Court supply depended on particular production arrangements
phases.text: The marker begins the conventional Ming period, not a precisely dated workshop foundation. phases.title: An order could cross the boundary between kiln organizations
phases.text: The CUHK account places allocation of court orders to capable private kilns in the Jiajing period when imperial capacity was insufficient. phases.text: The Met cites contemporary records for jars with similar pond decoration in 1542. phases.title: A particular institution’s change did not end skilled production
phases.text: The Palace Museum exhibition reports that imperial-kiln operations ceased in 1608 and describes flourishing private production afterward. title: Ottoman makers: signatures, workshop remains and markets

summary: A named decorator, an official emblem, a painted dish and production remains reveal different parts of skilled work. Markets and commissions could overlap without assigning every maker to a palace or every object to one known workshop.

phases.text: The British Museum records AH 956/1549, Iznik and Musli in its account of the lamp’s inscription. The supplied translation identifies a painter. phases.title: Drawing and illumination make an official emblem
phases.text: The Met distinguishes a specialist drawing the standard form from an illuminator decorating certain imperial documents. The marker begins the selected emblem’s approximate catalogue range, not every document’s issue date or the moment the tughra form was invented.

phases.title: Unfinished tiles connect a product to making
phases.text: The excavation authors compare six tile finds with seventeenth-century buildings in Istanbul. Kiln debris, firing equipment and unfinished pieces support production questions. phases.title: A buyer’s setting enters the evidence
phases.text: The Ashmolean teaching course excerpts John Covel describing a weekly market, local ceramic materials and vessels in use. This is a particular observer’s account, not a workshop census. title: Mughal book projects: making, translation and changing patrons

interval.label: Selected manuscript-project orientation, c.1562–1617 CE
interval.note: A selected project frame from the V&A’s approximate Hamzanama production convention to a separately catalogued 1616–17 Razmnama patronage example. phases.label: c.1562–1577: an approximate production convention
phases.title: A large illustrated project brings specialists together
phases.text: The V&A places the Hamzanama project approximately within these years while acknowledging contradictory contemporary volume counts and unstated exact dates. It describes writing, calligraphy and painting as related work. This is another manuscript project, not the selected Harivamsa folio or its recovered team.

phases.label: 1582: the commission reported in the catalogue
phases.title: A Sanskrit epic enters a Persian translation project
phases.text: The British Library catalogue dates Akbar’s commission of the Mahabharata’s Persian translation to 1582 and the first illustrated Jaipur copy to c.1585–86. Commission, translation and a later manuscript copy are not one date; neither dates the epic’s narrated events.

phases.label: 1585: a change in principal residence
phases.title: The court atelier is associated with Lahore
phases.text: The Met’s essay describes Akbar adopting Lahore as his principal residence in 1585 and places the royal atelier first at Fatehpur Sikri, then Lahore. The selected painting’s own catalogue still says probably Lahore. A court move does not convert that qualified attribution into a proven findspot or a precise itinerary.

citations.locator: Fatehpur Sikri/Lahore and royal atelier paragraphs

phases.label: 1587: the preface discussed by Pye
phases.title: Translation is framed through imperial religious authority
phases.text: Pye interprets Abu al-Fazl’s dated Razmnama preface as linking inquiry into religious truth with Akbar’s sovereign authority. This is an interpretation of an elite text, not measurement of universal agreement or a date when one fully formed policy began.

phases.label: c.1590–95: the selected folio’s visible catalogue date
phases.title: A Harivamsa story is made visible in paint
phases.text: The Met dates the selected Krishna/Govardhan folio approximately to 1590–95. The V&A separately places completion of the Harivamsa’s Persian translation around 1590, with illustrations added. These accounts do not identify an exact day, all stages of this leaf or the historical date of a sacred event.

phases.label: 1616–17: a different copy and named patron
phases.title: A courtier supports a later illustrated book
phases.text: A separately catalogued Razmnama folio belongs to a 1616–17 project for Abd al-Rahim, a commander and literary patron. It shows patronage continuing beyond the Akbar case. Its patron, painter and page history are not transferred to the selected Harivamsa.

title: New Julfa: forced settlement, work and surviving family records

interval.label: Selected New Julfa records, 1604–1747; final letter is later comparison
interval.note: A frame for selected events and differently dated records, not a community’s lifespan or a political boundary. The complete Isfahan capital-phase case remains 1598–1722. The 1747 family letter is explicitly later than that case; a seventeenth-century carpet, an individual firm’s records and modern source publications have separate dates.

summary: Coerced movement and unequal households belong beside skilled making and commercial coordination. Dated records reveal particular people and relationships, without supplying one experience for all Armenians or identifying the selected carpet’s makers.

citations.locator: Origin, settlement, and population; Society and administration

phases.label: 1604: destruction and forced movement from Old Julfa
phases.title: Commercial importance followed coercion
phases.text: Ghougassian describes the destruction of Old Julfa and forced Armenian relocation during the Ottoman–Safavid war. Later privileges or prosperity do not make the movement voluntary. The account distinguishes the circumstances of merchants from those of other deportees; no settled mass-deportation total is supplied here.

phases.label: 1605: settlement begins at New Julfa
phases.title: A new quarter required buildings and everyday work
phases.text: The Iranica account places the beginning of New Julfa’s settlement in early summer 1605 on the southern bank of the Zayandarud. Houses and churches formed part of a community built after forced movement. This date is distinct from the conventional 1597–98 capital transfer and does not date every surviving building.

citations.locator: Origin, settlement, and population: early summer 1605
Isfahan as the Safavid Capital: gradual development

phases.label: 1655–1659: a later movement of Armenian artisans
phases.title: Settlement did not end state-directed displacement
phases.text: Ghougassian identifies later expulsions of Armenian artisans from Isfahan and movement toward New Julfa in 1655–1659. This is a different episode from the 1604 deportation. It should not be merged into one journey or made the assumed biography of every craft household.

phases.label: 1656: funds pooled in one family firm
phases.title: A particular business joined capital and travelling agents
phases.text: Tajiryan’s selected account dates the Girach-Mirman brothers’ pooling of funds in New Julfa to 1656. It describes partnerships between capital holders and travelling agents, coordinated through commercial information. This particular gem-trading firm is not evidence for every household’s organization or a transaction involving the Doria carpet.

citations.locator: Family-firm paragraph; Commenda Contracts and Agents

phases.label: 1700: a translated letter negotiates turquoise prices
phases.title: Information was part of commercial work
phases.text: The paper presents a 1700 exchange between Herapet di Martin and Amirbēk di Vardan about the price and availability of turquoise. It exposes a practical disagreement, rather than a smooth, automatic flow of goods. The supplied translation does not establish a carpet shipment, complete route or the behavior of all merchants.

phases.label: 1747: a later family letter, outside the atlas case interval
phases.title: A household message adds another perspective on separation
phases.text: The UCLA account supplies passages from Anna Khatoon’s letter to her husband, a textile merchant, including family news and a request for his safe return. Its rendered date is 9 August 1747. This is a later comparison with the 1598–1722 case, not an eyewitness account of 1604 or a voice representing every woman.

title: Bukhara: making books and sustaining urban institutions

interval.label: Sixteenth–seventeenth-century bookwork and urban institutions
interval.note: Century-level orientation for selected manuscript work, restored teaching spaces, foundations and water infrastructure; not the city’s or a polity’s lifespan. The complete original 1500–1785 case and the selected folio’s ca.1525–35 range remain separate. Building ranges and restoration years do not recover a timetable for every teacher, maker or water worker.

summary: Books, classrooms, markets and reservoirs required continuing work. A painted folio, architectural descriptions and records of endowed property reveal different tasks and interests within a changing city.

citations.locator: Selected sixteenth/seventeenth-century building and restoration passages

phases.label: 1530s: a probable painting setting
phases.title: A copied text acquires a painted reception
phases.text: The Met places the manuscript’s painting probably in Bukhara in the 1530s, after likely copying in Herat. The decade marker is an orientation within the retained ca.1525–35 catalogue range, not a recovered manufacture year. The much older poem and modern photograph keep their own dates.

citations.locator: Description; visible date and qualified geography

phases.label: 1535–36: Mir-i Arab construction
phases.title: Teaching gains another built setting
phases.text: The architectural account dates Mir-i Arab to 1535–36. It belongs to a city with older teaching institutions, rather than the invention of learning there. This range does not establish an exact opening day, a complete curriculum or every student’s experience.

phases.label: 1585: restoring an older madrasa
phases.title: Continued use can require repair
phases.text: The Ulugh Beg madrasa was built in 1417, outside this reference frame, and restored in 1585. Its described courtyard, cells, classroom and mosque connect education to material spaces. Restoration is a separate event from the building’s first construction.

citations.locator: Ulugh Beg madrasa: plan description and restoration

phases.label: 1619–23: the Lab-i Hauz complex
phases.title: Water storage joins institutions and public space
phases.text: The architectural synthesis groups a khanaqah, madrasa and reservoir within a 1619–23 building range. The marker uses that range’s later edge. It does not reconstruct every canal connection, worker or resident’s right to draw water.

phases.label: 1671: a foundation known through a written record
phases.title: An endowment can outlast its buildings
phases.text: McChesney cites a document for Ay Padshah Bibi’s madrasas and water tank in 1671 among works no longer surviving as buildings. His account connects physical provision to endowed resources, while leaving the original deed and its precise obligations for further consultation.

citations.locator: Monuments and public works: Ay Padshah Bibi

title: Shiraz and changing rule: a selected Zand political sequence

interval.label: Selected political orientation, 1747–1794 CE
interval.note: Selected milestones from Perry’s account, beginning with Nader Shah’s assassination and ending with the last Zand ruler’s defeat. This reference does not replace the complete 1751–1794 case or date all Iranian life, lacquer production or the selected object’s use. Authority changed and had territorial limits; the frame is not a uniform national border.

summary: Karim Khan made Shiraz a residence and building center within a contested political landscape. His death preceded the selected lacquer case by ten years. The later succession provides orientation without assigning the case to a ruler, purchaser or workshop city.

citations.locator: Opening chronology; Karim Khan; succession to 1794

phases.label: 1747: a political rupture
phases.title: Nader Shah’s death precedes the Zand convention
phases.text: Perry begins Karim Khan’s rise within the struggles following Nader Shah’s assassination. This earlier reference point explains the selected sequence; it does not move the case’s preserved 1751 starting boundary.

citations.locator: Opening account of 1747 and Karim Khan’s rise

phases.label: 1751: the dynastic convention begins
phases.title: The title wakil represents authority
phases.text: Perry’s dynastic account uses 1751–1794 and describes Karim Khan’s adoption of the title wakil rather than shah. A deputy’s title did not eliminate executive power, campaigns or limits to the territories under his authority.

citations.locator: Karim Khan, the Wakil: title and limits of rule

phases.label: 1765–1779: residence at Shiraz
phases.title: A court, commercial work and building gather in one city
phases.text: Perry dates Karim Khan’s residence at Shiraz to these years and describes the citadel, mosque, gardens and covered bazaar, merchants and artisans. This urban context does not identify the manufacturing place of a case catalogued only as Iranian.

citations.locator: The Wakil at Shiraz, 1765–79: residence and urban work

phases.label: 1779: Karim Khan dies
phases.title: Succession changes the political setting
phases.text: Karim Khan’s death was followed by struggles among Zand successors. The selected case’s catalogue date, 1789, belongs to this later period; no surviving ownership record was established in this consultation.

phases.label: 1789: separate political and object dates
phases.title: Lotf Ali Khan’s accession and a dated case
phases.text: Perry dates Lotf Ali Khan’s rule from 1789; the Met separately dates Muhammad Baqir’s case 1204 AH/1789 CE. Their shared year supplies chronology, not evidence that this ruler commissioned or owned the case.

phases.label: 1794: the selected dynastic endpoint
phases.title: The last Zand ruler is defeated
phases.text: Perry ends the dynastic convention with Lotf Ali Khan’s defeat and execution. This political endpoint does not establish when a case ceased to be used or when a craft tradition ended.

citations.locator: Lotf Ali Khan’s defeat and execution in 1794

title: Pacific exchange: a wreck, shipbuilding and a later Mexican jar

interval.label: Selected exchange and work records, 1565–1726
interval.note: An orientation for selected evidence, not the full trade’s duration or a universal voyage. The complete original case remains 1565–1815. The 1595 wreck, separate 1618/1619 official accounts, ca. 1680–1700 Mexican jar and a 1726 registered consignment are different records. The reference ends with that selected registration, not the trade’s endpoint.

summary: Commodity movement depended on ships, materials and people. A particular interrupted voyage and official reports make some work visible; a later Mexican jar belongs to a different episode within the longer exchange history.

citations.locator: Title convention and short route/cargo account

phases.label: 1565: the retained trade convention begins
phases.title: A long commercial frame contains different episodes
phases.text: The Met essay and Point Reyes collection account use the 1565–1815 convention. This opening marker does not identify a particular cargo or make every journey follow an identical track. The selected reference stops earlier than the complete case.

phases.label: 1595: the San Agustín voyage is interrupted
phases.title: A wreck and village finds give a particular context
phases.text: The San Agustín, sailing from the Philippines toward Mexico, wrecked at tamál-húye, present-day Drakes Bay. Written accounts and objects recovered in Coast Miwok village contexts support a bounded inquiry. They do not turn the much later selected jar into wreck cargo or establish one exact route for the whole trade.

phases.label: 1618: a governor reports burdens of royal shipbuilding
phases.title: A colonial report links ships to fields and communities
phases.text: Fajardo’s letter of 10 August 1618 describes workers drawn from cultivation, harsh conditions and contributions from their communities. His contrasting claim about consenting labor concerns smaller private ships for regional navigation. It is an official’s argument about royal service and cost, not a survey of every worker or a proof that instructions changed conditions.

citations.locator: Fajardo letter: royal and private shipbuilding passages

phases.label: 1619: Pineda’s report, as editorially attributed
phases.title: Craft tasks and unpaid labor appear together
phases.text: The edition attributes Pineda’s report to [Mexico? 1619]. It identifies woodcutting, carpentry, mast-making and smithing, while reporting pay arrears and people leaving. The report covers ships, galleys and defense; it does not provide one galleon’s complete crew or prove that its wage schedules were paid.

citations.locator: Pineda: heading; Those who cut these woods; And because, they have; smiths

phases.label: ca. 1680–1700: a separate Mexican jar
phases.title: The selected object belongs to a later material history
phases.text: The Met dates accession 11.87.36 to approximately 1680–1700 and identifies Mexican tin-glazed earthenware. This is later than the 1595 wreck and remains distinct from imported Chinese porcelain. The catalogue does not identify its particular buyer, contents or voyage.

citations.locator: Artwork Details: Date, Geography, Medium and Object Number

phases.label: 1726: a particular registered consignment
phases.title: A named ship’s record gives a more specific connection
phases.text: Caño Ortigosa and Lee study the Santo Cristo’s register dated at Cavite on 26 June 1726 for a voyage to Acapulco. Their discussion follows Julián Ignacio’s entry for lacquered furnishings, ceramics described as Japanese and personal belongings. The registration does not identify this Mexican jar or establish every good’s precise origin, route, sale or successful delivery.

citations.locator: PDF 4 note 5; PDF 14: Julián Ignacio discussion

title: Banda: trade, coercion and continuing communities

interval.label: Selected trade and displacement evidence, 1599–1630
interval.note: A selected reference around the unchanged 1621 event case, not the beginning or end of Bandanese history. The final marker is a dated colonial observation of communities in Kei, not their first existence. The separate 2019 and 2021 sources concern modern language, remembrance and public claims; they are not eyewitness accounts of 1621.

summary: Monopoly required more than a contract: control of land, food and labor changed lives. Surviving communities continued work, relationships and remembrance beyond the campaign.

phases.label: 1599: Dutch visitors enter an existing trading society
phases.title: A trading port precedes the company’s monopoly
phases.text: Mostert and Manuhutu describe the first Dutch visitors paying port dues and exchanging goods for nutmeg and mace. This encounter did not create Bandanese commerce or establish a monopoly in practice.

phases.label: 1609: occupation and fortification intensify conflict
phases.title: Company trading claims acquire military force
phases.text: The National Archives account places the occupation of Neira and construction of a fort in the escalation toward conquest. Treaties and company claims must be distinguished from the choices and trading practice of the communities targeted.

phases.label: 1621: removal, hunger and enslavement
phases.title: The event case examines a policy of forced displacement
phases.text: The archive presents the council’s removal decision of 24 April and Coen’s report captioned 6 May. Its account characterizes the campaign as genocide. These records expose official purposes and resistance; they do not supply the full experience of those attacked or one settled casualty count.

citations.locator: Genocide: 24 April decision; 6 May report and modern Dutch renderings

phases.label: 1622: persecution and forced work continue
phases.title: The campaign’s consequences exceed one year
phases.text: Mostert and Manuhutu trace renewed persecution and forced transfers after 1621. Their account connects plantation production with the cultivation and processing knowledge of enslaved Bandanese people. The 1621 case date is not an endpoint for these consequences.

phases.label: 1630: a colonial encounter records a community in Kei
phases.title: Displacement is not disappearance
phases.text: The PALA account reports that VOC visitors encountered Bandanese people in the Kei region in 1630. It also describes continuing diaspora trade and political initiatives. The record is evidence of presence at that encounter, not a precise migration route, founding date or complete family history.

title: Textile work, schooling and inspection: selected 1833–1836 records

interval.label: Selected statute and enforcement evidence, 1833–1836
interval.note: This reference is an evidence sequence around the unchanged case, not industrialization’s lifespan or a claim that all factories changed together. The Act’s passage and commencement provisions are different dates. Quarry Bank provides broader background; the Science Museum’s catalogued 1927 machine is later and is not placed within these phases.

summary: A rule needed people, records and institutions to operate. These selected sources distinguish covered work, statutory obligations, an inspector’s investigation and contested evidence of results.

citations.locator: Lesson PDF, printed p. 9, Source 1 transcript

phases.label: 1833: the Act is passed
phases.title: 29 August dates a statute, not completed workplace change
phases.text: The Act names powered textile processes and regulates children and young persons through restrictions, schooling, certification and inspection. Its exceptions and commencement provisions matter. Its title does not turn it into a ban on all child work or a complete protection for every worker.

citations.locator: PDF 1: title/date and clause I; selected provisions

phases.label: 1834: selected provisions begin; others are phased
phases.title: The date of passage differs from implementation dates
phases.text: Clauses I and VII specify 1 January 1834 for their restrictions; clause VIII phases further age coverage over later months and contains a silk proviso. These are statutory instructions, not a measured series of compliance. The draft does not replace their detail with one universal daily-hours number.

citations.locator: PDF 1, clause I; PDF 3, clauses VII–VIII

phases.label: 1836: Parliament debates enforcement and alteration
phases.title: Reports become evidence in a contested political decision
phases.text: On 9 May, speakers disputed the law’s operation and a proposed change. Hindley quoted Inspector Howell describing instances of benefit, especially reduced night work; other speakers raised household earnings and practical difficulties. A parliamentary argument is not a neutral national compliance survey.

phases.label: 1836: an inspector describes a particular investigation
phases.title: A reported complaint requires evidence about what followed
phases.text: The institution dates the Taylor, Ibbotson & Co. extract to 1836. The inspector reports questioning boys, looking at a time book and intending punishment. The selected transcription does not provide ages, every break, the book’s findings or a completed penalty; it cannot alone measure all workplaces.

title: Silk work: learning, adaptation and the limits of protection

interval.label: Selected mill, training, storage and legal changes, 1872–1916
interval.note: A selected source frame from Tomioka’s opening to Factory Act implementation, extending four years beyond the Meiji period. It is not the mill’s operating lifespan or the beginning/end of Japanese industrialization. The earlier 1863 farmhouse and a later 1917 worker recollection are explicitly contextual comparisons. The original exact October 1872 case remains unchanged. Memoir writing/publication, modern scholarship, heritage listing and digitization have separate dates.

summary: Imported machinery depended on trained hands, local materials and people raising silkworms. Learning and technical change could coexist with restrictive working arrangements and incomplete legal protection.

phases.label: October 1872: the model mill opens
phases.title: A new mill uses established regional skills
phases.text: French machinery and advice met Japanese building work and an existing sericultural region. Opening the mill did not create the whole production system in one year or determine every employee’s later experience.

phases.label: 1874: trained workers teach at another mill
phases.title: Learning can travel through people
phases.text: The NDL places Wada Ei(ko)’s departure from Tomioka in July 1874 and subsequent teaching at Saijō, later Rokkōsha. Nakamura and Molteni discuss material changes at that separate Matsushiro mill through her later recollection. This is not an account freshly written during the visit or a reconstruction of Tomioka’s equipment.

phases.label: 1884: Takayama-sha becomes a school
phases.title: Controlling a living crop requires practice
phases.text: Students learned sericulture through practical rearing. Ventilation, warmth and humidity mattered to silkworms before cocoons reached a reel. The school’s date is distinct from the mill’s opening and from Tajima’s earlier 1863 farmhouse.

phases.label: 1905: Arafune’s first storage units operate
phases.title: Storage changes the timing of work
phases.text: Keeping eggs cool delayed hatching. Labels and catalogues helped staff return egg cards when needed. These early twentieth-century facilities did not exist at the mill’s 1872 opening, and their later functional association is not a mapped shipment itinerary.

phases.label: 28 March 1911: Factory Act promulgation
phases.title: Making a law and applying it have different dates
phases.text: The National Archives distinguishes the 1911 law from its later implementation. Protective provisions had a defined initial scope, rather than instantly covering every person working with silk.

phases.label: September 1916: implementation begins
phases.title: Protection needs evidence of how it works
phases.text: The law came into force after a five-year delay. Nakamura and Molteni describe exceptions affecting silk-reeling and evidence of continuing long hours in Nagano. This is a qualified regional comparison, not a finding that every Tomioka shift violated or complied with the law.

title: Photographic investigation, child-labor rules and enforcement in the United States

interval.label: Selected campaign and federal-administration frame, 1904–1918 CE
interval.note: An orientation frame from the NCLC’s founding through a particular federal act’s operation and constitutional reversal. It preserves the selected case’s complete 3 December 1908 interval. The 1921 report publication and 2019 institutional interpretation are later evidence clocks, not extensions of this frame. This is neither the beginning of all US labor organizing nor the end of child labor.

summary: Investigators made working conditions visible through photographs, captions, reports and exhibits. Enforcing age and hour rules required different work: checking evidence, issuing certificates and inspecting workplaces. A campaign, a statute and its administration answer different questions.

citations.locator: Background and Scope; The Photo Captions

phases.label: 1904: the institutional founding date
phases.title: An organization assembles a reform campaign
phases.text: The Library of Congress dates the NCLC’s founding to 1904. Its collection account describes investigation and publicity aimed at working children’s conditions. Founding one organization is not the origin of every labor campaign or proof that all families shared its program.

phases.label: 3 December 1908: the catalogued photograph date
phases.title: A particular mill scene enters a documented series
phases.text: The selected catalogue caption places the spinner at Mollahan Mills, Newberry, and reports the overseer’s denial. A separate group caption from that mill is also dated 3 December 1908. Related records allow comparison without making either picture a census, a verified age record or the same view.

citations.locator: Existing photo; indexed caption title, Hine 358 / nclc.01451

phases.label: 1913: a change in Hine’s NCLC role
phases.title: Photographs circulate through exhibits as well as print
phases.text: The collection account dates Hine’s promotion to head of the exhibits department to 1913. It describes photographs circulating in reports, publications, slide shows and displays. These uses explain intended audiences and publicity work; they do not measure each viewer’s response.

citations.locator: Background and Scope: distribution and exhibits

phases.label: 1 September 1916: approval of a particular act
phases.title: Congress links product shipment to age and hour conditions
phases.text: The Keating-Owen Act restricted interstate or foreign shipment of specified products made under prohibited child-employment conditions. It authorized inspections and provided for certificates. Its enactment was a legal step with a defined reach, not a direct result established for this single photograph or proof of compliance.

phases.label: 1 September 1917: the act takes effect
phases.title: Age evidence becomes an administrative task
phases.text: The Children’s Bureau report identifies this effective date. Its certificate discussion explains why trustworthy age evidence and coordination with state systems mattered. The report distinguishes those administrative arrangements from simply printing an age rule.

phases.label: Spring 1918 inspections; 3 June constitutional decision
phases.title: Inspection findings and a court ruling change the inquiry
phases.text: The report records underage employment and certificate gaps in a defined South Carolina inspection sample before the act was declared unconstitutional on 3 June. It also records later investigations under other authority and longer hours at the South Carolina factories revisited. This is a particular observed sequence, not proof that every protection or inspection ceased.

title: Communal work and the later interpretation of a Blackfoot hunting landscape

interval.label: Selected later-hunting frame and later source/heritage dates, 1700–2008
interval.note: The opening retains the atlas’s selected c.1700–1850 inquiry; it does not establish the first hunt. Later phases date heritage recognition, a photograph’s publication and an archaeological book, not continued hunting through 2008. The much longer site chronology and its interruption remain distinct; seasonal tasks are not assigned invented calendar years.

summary: Preparing and coordinating a hunt, processing materials and storing food connected a cliff with camps and household work. Community-authored teaching, a modern landscape view and archaeological interpretation supply different kinds of evidence across different dates.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis:long site history and interruption

phases.label: c.1700: opening of the selected atlas inquiry
phases.title: A teaching boundary, not an origin
phases.text: This opening inherits the dossier’s bounded later context. UNESCO describes a much older hunting landscape with an extended interruption; no particular eighteenth-century hunt or continuous identity of all earlier users is dated here.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis:long chronology and interrupted hunting

phases.label: c.1850: UNESCO’s later use boundary for this site
phases.title: A site endpoint does not end a people’s knowledge
phases.text: UNESCO gives an approximate 1850 endpoint in its site-use description. The community teaching accounts explain continuing cultural knowledge; this site boundary is not the end of Blackfoot people, all bison hunting or every community’s history.

phases.label: 1981: World Heritage inscription
phases.title: Recognition is a later institutional event
phases.text: The interpretive-site history and UNESCO identify 1981 inscription. This dates heritage recognition, not construction of drive lanes or the beginning of community care for the landscape.

phases.label: 2005: publication of the landscape photograph
phases.title: A modern surface view has a particular source history
phases.text: Commons records UM’s own photograph uploaded 17 July 2005 and a public-domain dedication. The picture is a later view, not a photograph of a hunt; camera metadata is not independent verification of an exact exposure date.

phases.label: 2008: publication of Brink’s archaeological study
phases.title: An experiment tests a question about processing
phases.text: Brink’s chapter 7, printed pp. 195–198, distinguishes a modern grease-processing experiment from a recovered ancient meal. Its cattle bones and modern tools remain part of its method, rather than disappearing from the explanation.

title: Hidatsa gardens, village relocation and continuing knowledge

interval.label: Selected village, recollection and displacement records, 1600–1954
interval.note: Big Hidatsa’s original c.1600–1845 case remains exact. Later Like-a-Fishhook recollections, 1917 publication, 1953 dam completion and 1954 relocation belong to this separate reference. Different villages have distinct occupations; no continuous occupation of one place or end of Hidatsa people is implied.

summary: Women’s cultivation, houses and storage supported households and exchange. Disease, relocation and government projects changed the settings in which people carried this knowledge; later records do not become direct witnesses to every earlier village.

citations.locator: Village & Relocations; Elbowoods & Garrison Dam Relocations

phases.label: c.1600: selected Big Hidatsa occupation begins
phases.title: One village has its own frame
phases.text: NPS places establishment of Big Hidatsa around 1600. Neighboring Awatixa villages have different histories; this is not the beginning of Hidatsa people or all cultivation in the region.

phases.label: 1837: epidemic and village reorganization
phases.title: A trading region also carried danger
phases.text: MHA’s selected history describes the smallpox epidemic and subsequent consolidation of village survivors. NPS connects the epidemic with river travel. The accounts do not supply one identical household experience or a precise mortality total adopted here.

phases.label: 1845: Like-a-Fishhook established upriver
phases.title: Relocation did not end community knowledge
phases.text: MHA identifies Núeta and Hiraacá establishing Like-a-Fishhook. This changes the place of residence and the case’s village frame; it does not end gardening, family relationships or Hidatsa identity.

phases.label: 1917: publication of a woman’s mediated agricultural account
phases.title: Remembered gardens are later evidence
phases.text: The University of Minnesota book presents Maxi´diwiac’s recollections through Goodbird’s interpretation and Wilson’s editing. The foreword describes 1912 recording and later corrections. Her Like-a-Fishhook memories are not a direct transcript of earlier Big Hidatsa life.

phases.label: 1953: Garrison Dam completed, in NPS’s account
phases.title: River engineering changed the conditions of life
phases.text: The NPS account describes the dam and flooding of reservation land despite tribal objections. The construction milestone is separate from MHA’s date for completed relocation the following year.

phases.label: 1954: relocation completed, in MHA’s account
phases.title: Displacement disrupted bottomland households
phases.text: MHA describes families moved from fertile bottomlands, communities dismantled and people scattered across new tracts. Its account places relocation completion in fall 1954. These losses do not authorize a story that the communities vanished.

title: Kwakwaka’wakw witnesses, prohibition and particular returns

interval.label: Selected law, community institution and return records, 1884–2003
interval.note: The complete original 1884–1980 case remains unchanged. Later returns in this reference do not move its endpoint, establish that every belonging returned or date the origins of potlatch. The 1884 amendment and 1885 commencement are distinct; 1980 opening and a particular 2003 return are separate events.

summary: Witnesses, family work and care for belongings give potlatch its consequences in the public explanations selected here. Prohibition, confiscation and return changed circumstances without making government or museum custody the sole authority over community knowledge.

citations.locator: Start and End of the Potlatch Ban

phases.label: 1884: amendment in U’mista’s history
phases.title: A law targets an institution
phases.text: U’mista dates the amendment to 1884. This is a government action against an existing practice, not the beginning of potlatch or evidence that people stopped participating.

phases.label: 1885: law takes effect in Living Tradition’s account
phases.title: Commencement is a different date
phases.text: Living Tradition gives 1 January 1885 for the prohibition taking effect. The two dates answer different questions about the legislation.
