title: Saint-Domingue and Haiti: emancipation, work and political authority

interval.label: Selected revolutionary decisions and records,1791–1804
interval.note: A phased source inquiry, retaining the complete original case interval unchanged. The boundaries connect an uprising to independence, not the lifespan of Haitian people or a completed transition to equal land, work or political rights. Later recognition/debt and 1825 comparisons are not incorporated without separate verified sources.

summary: Resistance, provincial emancipation, military allegiances, constitutional work rules and independence were distinct changes. Their surviving records expose authority and practical stakes without recovering every cultivator’s experience or one uniform revolutionary intention.

phases.label: 1791: uprising in the northern plantation region
phases.title: Resistance did not begin everywhere in the same way
phases.text: Manigat distinguishes the northern uprising from different struggles and alliances in the West and South. Enslaved people acted within changing military and political circumstances; a later independence outcome does not prove one identical starting program.

phases.label: 1793: provincial emancipation measures
phases.title: Local struggle preceded the metropolitan decree
phases.text: The parliamentary account places Sonthonax’s northern proclamation on 29 August, followed by Polverel’s measures in other provinces. English Heritage’s brief overview instead says September for the northern measure. The discrepancy is retained in source notes; the provincial decisions are not collapsed into the separate 1794 decree.

citations.locator: Selected renewed scope; compressed northern chronology

phases.label: 1794: the French Convention decrees colonial abolition
phases.title: A rule still required political and military support
phases.text: The institutional account describes deputies from Saint-Domingue reaching the Convention and the 4 February abolition decision. A decree changes the formal legal claim; it does not itself document implementation in every place or remove the military threats that followed.

citations.locator: Le débat: delegation and Convention decision

phases.label: 1797: Louverture’s letter to Vincent
phases.title: A formerly enslaved leader defended a particular allegiance
phases.text: The catalogued 21 October letter seeks Vincent’s advocacy with the Directory, challenges racist allegations and affirms attachment to France. It is a particular leader’s argument, not proof that every formerly enslaved person agreed or that independence was already a fixed 1791 objective.

phases.label: 1801: abolition and controlled cultivation in one constitution
phases.title: Status, labor and government power were different questions
phases.text: Articles 1 and 3 retain a French connection while prohibiting slavery. Articles 14–16 insist on cultivation and authorize police regulation of cultivators’ movement. Article 28 grants Louverture life tenure. These provisions do not certify voluntary work, actual revenue shares or equal political participation.

phases.label: 1804: independence proclaimed at Gonaïves
phases.title: An official act also organized authority
phases.text: The Acte’s dateline is 1 January. Its assembled generals renounce France. The separately studied printed packet also authorizes Dessalines’s life governorship. An official declaration and a new allocation of state power do not amount to a direct record of every household’s freedom or consent.

title: Te Tiriti: negotiation, asserted authority and early enforcement

interval.label: Selected negotiations and early colonial conflicts, 1840–1846
interval.note: A bounded frame from the first signings through the Northern War, not the Treaty’s lifespan, the whole colonization of Aotearoa or a common outcome for all iwi and hapū. The original exact 1840 case interval remains unchanged. Earlier He Whakaputanga, later land institutions, twentieth-century inquiries and a 2025 speech have separate dates. The close of this frame does not end Māori authority or continuing disputes.

summary: Making copies, interpreting words and gathering marks did not settle how authority would work. Crown proclamations and subsequent enforcement need evidence distinct from the signing record.

citations.locator: Northern War findings in official release

phases.label: 5–6 February 1840: discussion and the first signing
phases.title: An agreement is heard, debated and marked
phases.text: Rangatira heard the Māori text and verbal explanations at Waitangi before the first signatures on 6 February. Supporting and opposing speeches concerned authority, land and relations with newcomers. A later complete text does not preserve every spoken assurance.

citations.locator: Initial discussions; proposed Treaty; first signatures

phases.title: One English sheet does not stand for every signing
phases.text: The Waikato-Manukau sheet is in English. Its first signing date is uncertain; an 11 April witness note is distinct from a 26 April Manukau signing. Some rangatira signed while Te Wherowhero declined. Neither choice describes every Waikato or Ngāti Whātua position.

phases.title: The Crown announces a claim before circulation ends
phases.text: The proclamation asserts British sovereignty over the islands while sheets are still circulating. Ōnuku’s 30 May signing followed this announcement. A proclamation records what the Crown claimed; it does not establish every community’s consent or prove the promises were fulfilled.

phases.title: Absence and refusal remain part of the record
phases.text: The source records a final signing near Kāwhia on 3 September. The sheets did not reach every community, and some rangatira refused. The end of collecting marks was not an agreement on every interpretation or a referendum of all inhabitants.

phases.label: 1844–1846: disputes and the Northern War
phases.title: Enforcing authority changes people’s lives
phases.text: Hōne Heke and his followers challenged British authority by cutting the flagstaff at Kororāreka. Armed conflict followed. The Tribunal’s later Te Raki inquiry found serious Crown breaches in this period, including attacks on pā and kāinga and harm to non-combatants. These are district-specific historical findings, not a story of one uniform Māori response.

title: Satellite projects, observation and institutions: selected 1955–1958 records

interval.label: Selected satellite planning, launch and institutional responses, 1955–1958
interval.note: A bounded reference inquiry around an exact 1957 event, not the lifetime of Sputnik 1 or a complete 1945–1991 Cold War account. The registry’s broader institutional framework remains open. Later webpage editions, archive catalogues and anniversary exhibits are source-publication clocks, not ancient/event phases.

summary: An international scientific program gave satellite work a shared timetable while state priorities organized funding, secrecy and competition. A proposal, a completed launch and later arguments about observation or institutions establish different things.

phases.label: 1955: a public US satellite program for the IGY
phases.title: A common scientific timetable also became competitive
phases.text: NASA’s account dates the White House satellite announcement to July 1955 and the Vanguard selection to September. These are program decisions before the launch; the IGY itself ran from July 1957 through December 1958.

phases.label: January 1957: Korolev requests a simpler project
phases.title: A plan names organizations and a hoped-for date
phases.text: The 5 January proposal requests April–June launches, coordination across ministries and a radio/optical tracking system. The launch actually occurred in October. Proposed work and completed work must be checked against different records.

phases.label: October 1957: launch, announcement and observation
phases.title: One event entered several institutional arguments
phases.text: The 4 October launch is distinct from the Pravda announcement catalogued for 5 October and the 29 October Commons debate. The debate records both observation work and disagreement over national priorities, without standing for all British responses.

phases.label: 1958: new US institutions; IGY continues
phases.title: Institutional changes followed rather than defined the launch
phases.text: NASA’s timeline distinguishes the July Space Act, NASA opening in October and the IGY ending in December. These later decisions belong to the reference frame; the case retains its exact 1957 launch interval.

title: Aegean centres and British farms: different Bronze Age settings

interval.label: c. 1900–1100 BCE · selected European settings
interval.note: A teaching frame connecting separately dated evidence, not the lifespan of one society. Cretan palaces, mainland Greek centres and British farms did not share one government or one collapse. Britain’s broader museum periodization is c. 2300–800 BCE. The Uluburun link offers a dated cargo comparison; it does not identify that ship’s origin or destination.

summary: Around 1900 BCE, centres such as Knossos and Phaistos concentrated work, goods and record keeping on Crete. Mainland Greek workshops and palaces later provide a different set of records and objects. In Britain, farms, fields and round houses belonged to another settlement pattern; metal tools coexisted with stone and flint. These settings let us ask who organized production and how materials moved, without turning an Aegean palace history into the history of every European community.

phases.text: The selected museum overview begins its Mycenaean frame around 1600 BCE. Mycenae, Tiryns, Thebes and Athens are named centres. Vessels found far away support circulation of goods; they do not reveal every trader or the route of one voyage.

phases.title: A Cretan destruction horizon
phases.text: Archaeological destruction on Crete is placed around 1450 BCE in the consulted account. The source leaves responsibility uncertain. This date should not be merged with later mainland destruction or used as a universal end to European exchange.

phases.title: Different settings around the snapshot date
phases.text: The mainland account describes destruction and decline in the late thirteenth century BCE. The British overview instead describes a much longer Bronze Age sequence of farms, field divisions and deposited objects. Comparing these accounts does not establish synchronized change or an identical cause.

title: Kuk: drainage and cultivation in New Guinea

interval.label: c. 2400–450 BCE · selected Phase 3 evidence
interval.note: Rounded orientation for the Phase 3 sequence, not proof of cultivation in every field in every intervening year. The published early range is 4350–3980 calibrated years before 1950 (about 2400–2030 BCE); the late range is 2700–2400 (about 750–450 BCE). This is a highland New Guinea setting, not a history of all Southeast Asia or Oceania.

summary: At Kuk in the upper Wahgi Valley, buried ditch networks show people altering wet ground for cultivation. Archaeologists distinguish early and later drainage episodes and compare Kuk with other highland sites. Draining soil could make land usable, but the surviving cuts do not name the workers, settle their land rights or reveal every crop. This agricultural history should be read alongside, rather than absorbed into, the later island settlements associated with Lapita pottery.

phases.title: Early Phase 3: a dated range
phases.text: The early ditch-network range is approximately 2400–2030 BCE. The opening year is a rounded edge of that range, not a known day when ditch digging began.

phases.title: Later drainage evidence
phases.text: The table places a later subphase around 750–450 BCE. The interval between the published subphases must not become a fabricated continuous list of annual events.

phases.title: An archaeological boundary, not the end of a people
phases.text: The selected late range ends here. The authors distinguish later phases and warn that other sites lack enough evidence to establish the same pattern of abandonment. Changing a field system does not by itself establish the disappearance of a community.
